A getaway is an act of escaping — moving away from a place or situation, usually quickly. The word captures the feeling of getting away from something, whether that's a crime scene or the stress of your daily life. It always involves leaving something behind.
Meaning 1: An Escape After a Crime

This is the most classic and vivid use of the word. When someone commits a crime — a bank robbery, for example — they need to flee the scene before the police arrive. That act of fleeing is called a getaway.

Examples:

  • "The robbers robbed the bank and made a quick getaway."
  • "The police caught the suspect before he could make his getaway."
  • "The getaway was carefully planned — they had a fast car waiting outside."

Key nuance: In this meaning, a getaway almost always implies urgency, speed, and a sense of danger. There's something illegal happening. It's not a casual departure — it's a desperate escape.

This meaning gave rise to two very common phrases you'll often hear:

  • Getaway car — the vehicle used by criminals to escape after committing a crime. "The police found the getaway car abandoned near the highway."
  • Getaway driver — the person whose specific job it is to sit behind the wheel and drive the criminals away from the crime scene. "He didn't go inside the bank — he was the getaway driver."
Meaning 2: A Short Holiday or Break

In everyday modern usage — and this is arguably the more common meaning you'll encounter in daily life — a getaway simply means a short trip or vacation, usually taken to relax and escape from the pressures of normal life.

Think of it this way: just as a criminal "gets away" from the scene, you are "getting away" from your routine, your work, your stress.

Examples:

  • "We're planning a weekend getaway to the beach."
  • "After months of hard work, she needed a getaway."
  • "It was a romantic getaway — just the two of us in a cozy cabin in the mountains."
  • "Even a short getaway can do wonders for your mental health."

Key nuances for this meaning:

  • A getaway is generally short — a few days, not a month-long trip. If someone says "I'm going on a getaway," you picture a weekend or maybe a week, not a long holiday.
  • It carries a feeling of relief and escape — you're not just traveling; you're specifically getting away from something (stress, work, the city, routine).
  • It has a slightly spontaneous or indulgent feeling to it. It's a treat, a breather. Words like romantic, weekend, quick, and little are very commonly paired with it — a romantic getaway, a weekend getaway, a little getaway.
  • The destination is often somewhere peaceful, scenic, or different from where you live — a mountain cabin, a beach resort, a quiet town.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since the two meanings are quite different, context makes it very easy to tell them apart:

  • If the sentence involves crime, police, robbery, or fleeing, it's Meaning 1 (the escape after a crime).
  • If the sentence involves relaxation, travel, vacation, weekends, or a break, it's Meaning 2 (a short holiday).

You will almost never be confused in real life because the surrounding words make it obvious.
Common Words and Phrases Used With "Getaway"

Here are the most natural combinations you'll encounter:

  • Make a getaway — to successfully escape. "They made a clean getaway." (Usually crime-related.)
  • Weekend getaway — a short two-day vacation.
  • Quick getaway — either a fast escape (crime) or a brief holiday.
  • Romantic getaway — a trip for couples.
  • Plan a getaway — to organize either an escape or a trip.
  • A getaway destination — a place people go to relax and escape.
  • Getaway car / getaway driver — crime-related, as explained above.
The Emotional Flavor of the Word

One thing that makes "getaway" special is that both meanings carry a sense of freedom. Whether it's a criminal fleeing the police or a tired office worker heading to a mountain cabin, the word always suggests: I am leaving this behind. I am breaking free.

This is why it's such a popular and appealing word in travel advertising — "Plan your perfect getaway!" sounds far more exciting than "Plan your short trip!" The word promises an escape, a sense of liberation, a fresh breath of air.
